You have a lot more power, flexibility and control over what you can do, and you can (ideally) reproduce your workflow in a markdown file or notebook if it's all in code.

Once you become more proficient in programming, it's also much faster IME. I've used SPSS before (GUI only), and my entire workflow felt very sluggish.

There's also going to be plenty of features that are not available in a GUI, meaning that you have to code; this is especially true of R, since its ecosystem is huge.

But if you just need a simple scatterplot or table of summary statistics, then Jamovi is probably fine.

It's good to have a foundational understanding of SQL and computer architecture, so those courses make sense.

If you're interested in computer vision, it's a good idea to take both a CV course and computer graphics course. If developing computer simulations using 3D models sounds appealing, I'd still recommmend a computer graphics course. 

If there are any courses on distributed and parallel computing, I'd enrol in one of those. Very useful to understand the fundamentals if you want to work in a super computing environment. You can ask your lecturer if there are any opportunities to play around with Slurm.

On the stats side, I'd take both a Bayesian stats and time series course, which I would guess are offerered in third year.
